whyScene: The claim is a comparison across a parameter: as n grows, one and the same statistic gets less variable and more bell-shaped while the raw data does not change at all. A single static histogram of means has to pick one n; a side-by-side pair makes the learner remember the other case instead of seeing it. Driving n with one control and letting the bars morph, with the raw panel pinned and untouched beside it, keeps the means-versus-raw contrast and the 1 over square-root-of-n shrinkage on screen at the same moment.
layout: Left half: four grey bars (heights 200, 132, 84, 52) on the baseline y = 470 spanning x 96 to 350, labelled raw data. Right half: five blue bars at x 545, 613, 681, 749, 817, width 56, on the same baseline, whose heights are arithmetic functions of the property n, so the whole panel is one function of one control. A dashed grey normal curve peaks at (709, 340) as the large-n limit. Below the right panel a red standard-error bar runs from 545 to 545 + 260 over the square root of n.

beats.beat: Right panel introduced as the distribution of means.
n rises 3 to 10: outer means bars fall.
n rises to 30: shape approximates the dashed curve.
n = 60: standard error about a fifth of its start.

interaction.prompt: Which panel is the sampling distribution: the left or the right?
Did the spread of the means grow or shrink between n = 3 and n = 10?
Continue to n = 30 and watch the middle bar rise.
Is the distribution of means exactly normal at n = 60, and what does sigma over the square root of n do when n goes 9 to 36?

misconceptionMoves.move: The left-hand parent histogram is drawn once and has no track, so it is literally incapable of changing while n runs 3 to 60; only the right-hand panel, labelled sample means, moves.

misconceptionMoves.misconception: A larger n increases the standard error
misconceptionMoves.move: The red standard-error bar is an explicit function of n, 260 over the square root of n, so it can only shorten as the slider rises; the narration converts the length change into the numbers 1.73, 0.95 and 0.39.

correctnessChecks: Standard error falls monotonically with n: the red bar is 260 over the square root of n, from about 150 px at n = 3 to about 34 px at n = 60.
Every label and the narration name the right-hand panel as the distribution of the sample mean, never of the observations.
No exact normality claim: the dashed curve is labelled a limit, and the final checkpoint asks the learner to deny exactness at n = 60.
The bar heights are schematic densities, not simulated data, and the fallback text says so.
